Chapter 7: Changing Attitudes and the Rise of Multiculturalism
As the years rolled on, the arrival of migrants and their children started to do more than just reshape neighborhoods—they began to change the national conversation itself. The old idea that everyone needed to blend in, to leave their differences at the door, started to fade. By the 1970s, people were talking about something new: multiculturalism.
What did that mean for Australia? Well, it meant recognizing that our diversity could actually make us stronger, not just set us apart. But you know, this kind of change doesn’t happen overnight. For a long time, debates about immigration and what it means to “fit in” bubbled quietly in the background. Some folks worried that the country was moving too fast, that things they’d always relied on were slipping away. There were tough moments—politicians playing on fears, headlines painting migrants as outsiders. But there were also moments of joy: food festivals packed with people from every background, sports teams showing off Australia’s new face, and public figures proudly sharing their own migrant roots.
For many families who’d made the journey to Australia, this shift toward multiculturalism felt like a huge relief. Suddenly, the traditions and customs they’d held onto weren’t just private memories—they were seen as something valuable, something to be shared. A simple Sunday lunch, once just a way to remember home, became part of the bigger story of what it means to be Australian. Schools started offering language classes and hosting cultural days. Local councils backed festivals and supported community groups. The idea of belonging kept expanding, making space for new voices and fresh stories.
Of course, it wasn’t all smooth sailing. Some people worried that multiculturalism might pull communities apart, or leave some groups feeling left out. And let’s be honest—not everyone benefitted equally. Racism and exclusion were still real, sometimes showing up in ways that were hard to spot. Building a truly inclusive society takes time, patience, and—maybe most of all—a willingness to really listen to each other.
Even with these challenges, the move toward multiculturalism was a turning point. It gave Australia a new way to think about identity—not as something rigid or closed off, but as something that could grow, change, and welcome more people in. For the children and grandchildren of early migrants, this shift opened up new doors. They could finally see themselves as part of Australia’s story, without giving up where they’d come from.
